name: Ladin, varieties of Val di Fassa
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (0 state the same rule, 1 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Yang, Yifan, Rachel Walker, Alessandro Vietti & Armin Chiocchetti. 2021 [issue 2022]. Ladin, varieties of Val di Fassa. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 52(3): 495-520. doi:10.1017/S0025100320000262 (open access, Cambridge Core PDF).
catalog_quote: Word stress. In general, primary stress falls on one of the last three syllables in a word. Illustrations of stress in each of these positions are provided with words from Moenat. Final stress /kaˈs̠tra/ castrà 'castrated', /bonoˈrif/ bonorìf 'early ADJ'. Penultimate stress /ɲiˈɲɔla/ gnignola 'lizard', /ˈsez̠la/ sesla 'sickle'. Antepenultimate stress /ˈfemena/ fémena 'woman', /ˈt̠s̠aneva/ ciàneva 'cellar'. [p. 518] In the orthographic tradition that we follow here, the stressed syllable may be indicated by an accent mark. ... An accent is regularly marked in words ending in a vowel with stress on the final syllable and to indicate the pronunciation of words with vowel hiatus, such as /saˈuk/ saùch 'cricket, grasshopper; elder tree' (Brach), which is pronounced distinct from a diphthong /au/. An accent is often used in words ending in a vowel with stress on the antepenultimate syllable, and in words ending in a stem consonant with stress on the penultimate syllable, e.g. /ˈtsɛkol/ zécol 'stick' (Brach). ... According to these conventions, when no accent mark is present in a polysyllabic word, stress is most often penultimate. Further research is needed to gain insight into Ladin foot structure and any categorical or gradient influences of word shape on the locus of stress assignment.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Illustrations of stress in each of these positions are provided with words from Moenat. Final stress /kaˈs̠tra/ castrà 'castrated'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Romance-type lexical stress restricted to a three-syllable window at the right edge of the word (final, penultimate or antepenultimate); position is not predictable from the segmental string alone (orthography marks final stress on vowel-final words and often antepenultimate stress), with penultimate the most frequent pattern. The Gherdëina orthography (Forni, Istitut Ladin Micurà de Rü, 'L azënt') adds the distributional generalisation: vowel-final words mostly penultimate ('La majera pert dla paroles che tl gherdëina fina cun n vocal à l azënt tonich sun la penultima silba'), consonant-final words mostly final ('Chëles che fina cun n consonant à l azënt tonich n gran pert sun l'ultima silba'), with lexical exceptions (batum, Jevun, mefun).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in either source.
new_statements.exceptions: JIPA: vowel hiatus words like /saˈuk/ saùch carry an accent mark; accent marks also used for non-stress purposes (é vs e; Cazet pèrt). Forni (Gherdëina): some consonant-final words are not final-stressed (batum, Jevun, mefun, mesun, Sacun); verb forms with enclitics keep the base accent (SPELL 2001 p. 30).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level primary stress in citation forms; JIPA transcriptions of connected speech ('North Wind and the Sun') mark stress per word. JIPA data are from Val di Fassa varieties (Brach, Cazet, Moenat; stress examples from Moenat).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted JIPA statement describes the Val di Fassa varieties of Ladin (Fascian: Brach, Cazet, Moenat; stress examples from Moenat) = Glottolog dialect Fassano [fass1244] under ladi1250. The supporting Forni online orthography describes Gherdëina (Val Gardena) = Gardenese [gard1241]. SPELL 2001 describes the constructed written standard 'Ladin Dolomitan/Ladin Standard'. All fall under language-level ladi1250.

new_statements.quote: § 61. Die besten raetischen Mundarten dulden keine Proparoxytona, d. h. hinter dem betonten Vokale (oder der betonten Vokalgruppe) nur noch einen konsonantischen Verschluss, dann noch einen Vokal (oder eine Vokalgruppe) und endlich wieder einen konsonantischen Abschluss [...]. Wie weit dieses Gesetz herrscht, mag man in der unten stehenden Tabelle an dominica, femina und iuvenis (f.) beobachten. [p. 56] — Table, p. 57: 'Vigo doményǫ fémenǫ žóenǫ / o doményǫ fémenǫ žónǫ' — §153 p. 124: 'Der Vokal des Stammes [...] tritt meistens in zwei verschiedenen Lautformen auf, je nachdem der Wortton auf ihn oder auf die Endung fällt.'
new_statements.translation: §61. The best Rhaetic dialects tolerate no proparoxytones, i.e. after the stressed vowel (or stressed vowel group) only one more consonantal closure, then one more vowel (or vowel group) and finally a consonantal close again [...]. How far this law holds may be observed in the table below for dominica, femina and iuvenis (f.). [p. 56] — Table p. 57: Vigo [Lower Fassa] doményǫ 'Sunday', fémenǫ 'woman', žóenǫ 'young (f.)'; o [Upper Fassa: Canazei, Alba] doményǫ, fémenǫ, žónǫ. — §153 p. 124: The stem vowel [...] mostly appears in two different sound-shapes, according to whether the word stress falls on it or on the ending.
new_statements.citation: Gartner, Theodor. 1883. Raetoromanische Grammatik. Heilbronn: Henninger.
new_statements.locator: Lautlehre, Vokale '2. Unbetont', §61 p. 56 (archive.org leaf 112) and the dominica/femina/iuvenis table p. 57 (leaf 113), rows 'Vigo' and 'o' (= Ober-Fascha: Canazei, Alba); also §153 p. 124

The p. 57 table (page scan; scanned scrambles it) has the two Fassa rows 'Vigo doményǫ fémenǫ žóenǫ' and 'o doményǫ fémenǫ žónǫ' as claimed, next to p (Grö…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing Yang et al. 2021 statement (primary stress on one of the last three syllables, lexically fixed). Adds: (a) an 1883 attestation that Fassa (both Upper Fassa 'o' and Vigo) retains Latin proparoxytones (fémenǫ) where Gröden (p fánǫ), Badia (q3 fómna) and most Grisons dialects have lost them, i.e. antepenultimate stress is an old, genuine Fassa trait, not a loan pattern; (b) stem/ending stress alternation in verbs (§153). No contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gartner gives no stress rule of his own for Fassa; stress figures only as the conditioning factor for vowel development (chapter split 'Betont' / 'Unbetont'). His §61 law (no proparoxytones in the 'best' Rhaetic dialects) is explicitly tested in a table, and the two Fassa rows show that Fassa does NOT obey it: femina > fémenǫ keeps antepenultimate stress, while doményǫ and žónǫ are penultimate; elsewhere in the book Fassa words with final stress appear (§62 p. 57 Vigo gratadóǫ 'grater', o tšutšáǫ 'lime kiln'; §95 p. 74 Vigo, o tobiá 'hayloft'). So Fassa stress falls on any of the last three syllables, fixed lexically (etymologically), which is the catalog's reading. §153 adds that verb stems alternate between stem stress and ending stress across the paradigm.
new_statements.exceptions: §60 p. 56: particles used proclitically/enclitically vs 'mit einem eigenen Ton im Satze'; §33 p. 41: meus has shifted its Tonstelle in many dialects because it is so often proclitic; §94 p. 73: 'Tonversetzungen' (stress shifts) in -eolus derivatives, legere/regere derivatives, excitare etc. (Vigo mešédǫ 'stirs' listed); §14 p. 16: the German loan Kummet keeps German stress in f, t2 and o (Ober-Fascha).
new_statements.identity_note: Gartner 1883 treats Val di Fassa as two lects: siglum 'o' = Ober-Fascha (o1 Canazei, o2 Alba; Penia said to equal o2), counted among his core Rhaetic dialects (Einleitung pp. xxx-xxxi), and 'Vigo' = Vigo di Fassa (Unter-Fascha), which he deliberately leaves outside the core set as transitional toward Fleims/Trentino (Einleitung p. xxxiv). Moena (Moenat), the variety the JIPA illustration uses for its stress examples, is not one of his informant points. The p. 57 table gives identical stress placement for Vigo and o.

sources.note: Every word has a tonic accent; most vowel-final words are stressed on the penult (brama, chilo, sluseda), most consonant-final words on the final syllable (gurmel, madroz, patat), with some consonant-final exceptions not final-stressed (batum, Jevun, mefun); graphic accent mostly not.

sources.note: Ch. A.4 'L azent y l apostrof' pp. 28-30: purely orthographic rules (write the accent on every polysyllabic oxytone ending in a stressed vowel: starà, jené, proibì, aldò, palù; on certain verb forms; enclitics keep base accent). No statement of a default stress position.

tone.quote: The first of these features is accentual position: the questionnaire contains one name with the stress on the antepenultimate syllable (Berbora “Barbara”), two with the stress on the penultimate syllable (Madalena “Magdalene” and Fridl “Frederick”), and six with the stress on the last syllable [...]. [...] In sum, the intonation of Ladin chanted calls can be thought of as the result of three elements: an underlying L+H* !H% tune, the obligatory left-spreading of the !H% tone within the final syllable, and the right-spreading of the H* to the non-final unstressed syllables (if any).
